Can I Sleep on the Side Where My Implant Was Placed?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

After having a dental implant placed, many patients find themselves lying awake at night — not because of discomfort, but because of uncertainty. One of the most commonly searched questions following implant surgery is simply: "Can I sleep on the side where my implant was placed?" It seems like a straightforward question, yet the answer has real implications for your recovery, comfort, and long-term outcome.

Sleeping position is something we rarely think about until something changes — and a dental implant procedure is exactly that kind of change. The first few nights following surgery are a critical window in the healing process. Understanding why certain positions are recommended, and how sleeping on the implant side could affect recovery, can make a meaningful difference to how smoothly your body heals.

This article explains what happens to the implant site during those early days, what position is generally considered most supportive of healing, and when it may be appropriate to return to your usual sleeping habits. As always, individual recovery varies, and your dental team's specific guidance takes precedence.

Can You Sleep on the Side Where Your Dental Implant Was Placed?

In the initial days following dental implant surgery, it is generally advisable to avoid sleeping directly on the implant side. Sleeping on the treated side may increase localised swelling, pressure, and discomfort at the surgical site. Keeping your head elevated and resting on the opposite side can support more comfortable healing during the early recovery period.

Why Sleeping Position Matters After Dental Implant Surgery

When a dental implant is surgically placed into the jawbone, the surrounding tissue enters an active healing phase. The body sends increased blood flow to the area, which can cause swelling, tenderness, and sensitivity — particularly within the first 48 to 72 hours.

During sleep, the position of your head and face directly influences how localised blood and fluid pressure distributes around the surgical site. If you sleep on the same side as your implant, the contact pressure between your pillow and your cheek or jaw can:

  • Increase swelling in the surrounding soft tissue
  • Create mild but persistent pressure on the gum tissue at the implant site
  • Cause discomfort that disrupts sleep quality
  • Potentially disturb the wound if the site is still in the very early stages of closure

None of these outcomes are necessarily dangerous on their own, but they can slow the comfort of your recovery and make the first few nights more unpleasant than they need to be.

Sleeping on the opposite side — or on your back with your head gently elevated — removes direct pressure from the implant area and allows inflammation to settle more evenly. Most patients find this adjustment helpful for the first three to five days, with their normal sleeping habits gradually resuming as comfort allows.

What Happens to the Implant Site During the First Week?

Understanding the biology behind early implant healing helps explain why these precautions are clinically sensible.

A dental implant is a titanium post that is surgically inserted into the jawbone to replace the root of a missing tooth. Once placed, the body begins a process called osseointegration — the gradual fusion of the titanium surface with the surrounding bone tissue. This process is foundational to the long-term success of the implant and can take several months to complete fully.

However, the initial healing phase — covering the first seven to fourteen days — primarily involves soft tissue recovery. The gum around the implant site needs to close and stabilise. Blood clot formation is an important part of this process, protecting the underlying surgical area and allowing new tissue to regenerate.

Disruption to this early phase — whether through physical pressure, movement, or other disturbances — can occasionally slow soft tissue healing or cause unnecessary discomfort. For this reason, the advice around sleeping position, diet, and activity levels during the first week is specifically designed to protect this initial wound closure stage.

If you have had single tooth implant treatment in London, your treating clinician will have provided specific aftercare instructions tailored to your procedure. Always follow their guidance as the primary reference for your individual recovery.

Recommended Sleeping Positions After Implant Surgery

There is no universally mandated sleeping position prescribed by every implant surgeon, but there are generally agreed-upon principles that most clinical aftercare guidance reflects:

Sleep on Your Back Where Possible

Lying on your back distributes pressure evenly across the back of your head and keeps the face and jaw free from contact with a pillow. This is widely considered the most neutral position in the early post-operative period.

Elevate Your Head Slightly

Using an extra pillow to gently elevate your head above heart level can help reduce blood pooling in the face and jaw area. This simple adjustment is associated with less pronounced swelling during the first 48 hours.

Avoid Sleeping Directly on the Implant Side

Whether you prefer to sleep on your left or right side, try to choose the side that is opposite to where the implant was placed for the first few days. This removes sustained contact pressure from the healing gum tissue.

Transition Gradually

As swelling reduces and comfort improves — typically after the first week — most patients naturally return to their preferred sleeping positions without issue. There is no fixed timeline, and what matters most is that you feel comfortable and are not experiencing increased pain or swelling.

If sleeping positioning is affecting your rest significantly, mention this to your dental team at your follow-up appointment so they can assess your recovery and offer further guidance.

The Clinical Science: Osseointegration and Why Early Care Matters

To appreciate why aftercare in the first weeks is so important, it helps to understand what osseointegration actually involves at a biological level.

Titanium — the material used in most modern dental implants — is biocompatible, meaning the body does not treat it as a foreign object. Over a period of weeks to months, bone cells (called osteoblasts) grow directly onto the implant surface, forming a secure, stable anchor within the jaw. This process is what gives dental implants their characteristic durability and functional similarity to a natural tooth root.

Osseointegration cannot be accelerated, but it can be compromised if the implant experiences excessive early loading or micromovement during the initial phase. The implant itself is embedded in bone and is not directly affected by sleeping position in isolation — however, protecting the overlying soft tissue from unnecessary pressure and inflammation indirectly supports the conditions in which osseointegration proceeds optimally.

Osteoclasts (cells that break down bone) are also active during early healing as part of the remodelling process. A healthy healing environment — low in inflammation, free from infection, and well-rested — is one in which osteoblast activity is able to outpace disruption. This is why the cumulative effect of many small aftercare choices, including sleeping position, adds up to a meaningful difference in early recovery comfort.

Other Aftercare Considerations Alongside Sleeping Position

Sleeping position is just one part of a broader set of aftercare recommendations that support implant healing. The following areas are equally important during the early recovery period:

Diet and Chewing

Soft foods are recommended for the first several days to avoid placing biting or chewing forces on the implant site. Avoid very hot foods or drinks in the first 24 hours, as these can affect the healing tissue. If you are unsure about fizzy drinks during recovery, see our guide on sparkling water and dental implants.

Oral Hygiene

Keeping the mouth clean is essential, but the implant area itself should be managed gently in the early days. Your clinician will advise on when normal brushing near the site can resume and may recommend a chlorhexidine mouthwash to support gum health.

Avoiding Alcohol and Smoking

Smoking is known to negatively impact implant healing outcomes and is generally discouraged both before and after treatment. Alcohol should be avoided in the early post-operative period, particularly if prescribed antibiotics or pain relief are being taken.

Physical Activity

Strenuous exercise should be limited in the first few days, as elevated heart rate and blood pressure can increase swelling and post-operative bleeding at the site.

These recommendations work together. If you would like to understand more about the full process and timeline, booking an implant consultation is the most appropriate starting point.

When to Contact Your Dental Team

Most patients experience some degree of swelling, tenderness, and minor discomfort in the days following implant surgery. This is a normal and expected part of the healing process. However, there are certain signs that may indicate it is worth contacting your dental practice for further guidance:

  • Swelling that appears to be worsening beyond the third or fourth day, rather than gradually improving
  • Persistent or increasing pain that is not controlled by the pain relief recommended by your dentist
  • Signs of localised infection, such as discharge, an unpleasant taste, or heat around the site
  • Bleeding that does not settle with gentle pressure
  • Loosening or unusual movement at the implant crown or abutment
  • Fever or general malaise that seems connected to the surgical site

These symptoms, if present, should prompt a call to your dental team so they can assess whether further examination is needed. None of these symptoms necessarily indicate a serious complication — but they do merit professional evaluation rather than a wait-and-see approach at home.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

How Long Before I Can Sleep Normally Again?

This is one of the most reassuring aspects of implant aftercare: the period during which sleeping position matters is relatively short. For most patients, the first three to five days are the most critical window. After this point:

  • Soft tissue swelling typically begins to subside noticeably
  • Gum tissue around the implant begins to stabilise and firm up
  • Discomfort levels reduce, allowing more natural movement and positioning during sleep
  • The risk of pressure-related irritation at the site diminishes substantially

By the end of the first week, many patients have returned to sleeping in their usual position without any adverse effects. By two weeks, most patients report that their sleep is back to normal.

That said, individual healing timelines vary. Age, general health, the complexity of the surgical procedure, whether bone grafting was involved, and other factors can all influence how quickly recovery progresses. Your implant dentist will typically schedule a follow-up appointment within the first week or two specifically to assess healing progress.

If you are concerned about your recovery timeline, this is best discussed with your treating clinician, who can evaluate the site directly and provide personalised guidance.

Oral Health and Long-Term Implant Success

Once the early healing phase is behind you, maintaining long-term implant health becomes the focus. Unlike natural teeth, implants are not susceptible to decay — but the gum tissue and bone surrounding them absolutely can be affected by inadequate oral hygiene.

Peri-implantitis is a condition in which the gum and bone around a dental implant become inflamed, often as a result of plaque accumulation. If left unaddressed, it can lead to bone loss around the implant and, in more advanced cases, implant failure. It shares similarities with gum disease affecting natural teeth and is managed in comparable ways — with professional cleaning, improved home care, and in some cases, additional treatment.

Preventing peri-implantitis begins with the habits you establish after your implant is placed:

  • Brush twice daily using a soft-bristled toothbrush
  • Use interdental brushes or floss specifically designed for implants
  • Attend regular hygienist appointments for professional cleaning around the implant
  • Attend routine dental check-ups so the implant can be monitored over time

Understanding how to care for dental implants long-term is an important part of protecting your investment in your oral health.

Key Points to Remember

  • Avoid sleeping directly on the implant side during the first three to five days after surgery to reduce pressure and discomfort at the healing site.
  • Sleeping on your back with your head slightly elevated is widely considered the most comfortable and supportive position in the early post-operative period.
  • The early healing phase involves soft tissue closure and lays the foundation for osseointegration — the long-term fusion of the implant with the jawbone.
  • Most patients can return to normal sleeping habits within one to two weeks, as swelling and tenderness gradually subside.
  • Additional aftercare factors — including diet, oral hygiene, and avoiding smoking — are equally important during recovery.
  • Contact your dental team if swelling worsens after day three, if pain is not managed by recommended pain relief, or if you notice signs of infection.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will sleeping on my implant side cause the implant to fail?

Sleeping on the implant side for one night is unlikely to cause implant failure. Implants are secured within the jawbone and are not easily dislodged. However, repeated or sustained pressure on the gum tissue in the early post-operative days can increase swelling and discomfort, which may make your recovery more uncomfortable than necessary. Sleeping on the opposite side or on your back simply reduces the chance of this happening. If you are concerned about your specific situation, your dental team is best placed to advise you.

How do I manage swelling after dental implant surgery?

Swelling is a normal part of the body's healing response after implant surgery. Applying a cold compress to the cheek in the first 24 hours — in intervals of 10 to 15 minutes — can help reduce swelling. Keeping your head elevated while sleeping also helps. Most swelling peaks around the second or third day and then gradually reduces. If swelling continues to increase after day three or four, it is worth contacting your dental practice for guidance.

Can I use a regular pillow after implant surgery?

Yes, a regular pillow is fine. You may find it helpful to use an additional pillow to elevate your head slightly, which can reduce facial swelling. Some patients find a travel pillow or V-shaped pillow useful for keeping themselves positioned on their back during the night. There is no clinical requirement for a specific type of pillow — comfort and positioning are the primary considerations.

Is it normal to feel throbbing at the implant site at night?

Mild throbbing discomfort at the implant site — particularly at night when you are lying still and there are fewer distractions — is fairly common in the first two to three days following surgery. This is usually a normal aspect of soft tissue healing. Taking pain relief as recommended by your dentist and keeping your head elevated may help. If the throbbing is severe, persistent beyond the first few days, or accompanied by swelling or other symptoms, contact your dental practice for assessment.

When can I eat normally after dental implant surgery?

In the first few days, soft foods that require minimal chewing are recommended. Foods such as soup, yoghurt, mashed vegetables, and scrambled eggs are typically well tolerated. As comfort improves — usually within one to two weeks — a more varied diet can gradually resume. However, avoid very hard, crunchy, or sticky foods near the implant site until your dentist confirms that healing is progressing well, as these can place undue force on the area.

Does sleeping position matter after the healing period is complete?

Once full healing has occurred — which includes soft tissue recovery and the ongoing process of osseointegration over several months — sleeping position has no clinical relevance to implant health or longevity. The early post-operative period is the most important window during which sleeping position may affect comfort. After this, normal habits can resume without concern.

Conclusion

Recovering from dental implant surgery involves a number of small but meaningful adjustments to your daily routine — and sleeping position is one of them. In the first three to five days following the procedure, avoiding direct pressure on the implant side by sleeping on your back or the opposite side can help reduce swelling, protect the healing gum tissue, and make recovery more comfortable.

The underlying reasons for this guidance relate to the body's natural inflammatory response and the importance of protecting soft tissue healing during the initial phase of recovery. While sleeping position alone is unlikely to determine the success or failure of your implant, it is one of several straightforward steps that together support a smoother healing experience.

As soft tissue swelling subsides and comfort improves — typically within the first week — most patients find they are naturally able to return to their usual sleeping position. Every recovery is individual, and your dental team is the most reliable source of personalised aftercare guidance for your specific situation.

If you experience worsening symptoms, unusual pain, or any signs of infection, do not hesitate to contact your dental practice. Early assessment is always preferable to waiting when something does not seem right.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
